client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really stuck since my breakup with Maria. I used to love hiking with my friends, but now it just feels empty and pointless. I’m not sure if therapy can really help me get back to how I was before—it just feels like everything lost its meaning.
therapist: "I hear how painful this loss feels—how activities that once brought joy now feel empty. You sound like you're carrying a lot of energy when you talk about this, even while describing such heaviness. What thoughts come up when you notice that shift—from loving hiking to feeling it's pointless?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I keep thinking about how Maria would always be there waiting with coffee when I got back from hikes. Now when I'm out there, all I can think is "what's the point?" It's not just the hiking - everything feels duller now. Like all the color got drained from my life.
therapist: "It sounds like Maria's absence has become especially vivid during these routine moments that used to include her. When you notice everything feeling duller now, does that thought 'what's the point?' come with any specific images or memories?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I keep seeing her smiling when I'd come back sweaty from the trail, how she'd pretend to be grossed out but still hug me anyway. It just makes me angry now—why can't I enjoy things without her? But also... I don't know if I want to enjoy things without her, if that makes sense? Like moving on feels like betraying what we had.
therapist: "There's real tension here—holding onto those sweet memories feels important, yet the thought of creating new joys stirs up guilt. When you describe that conflict between anger and loyalty, where do you feel it most in your body?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's like this heavy weight in my chest that won't go away. Sometimes when I think about going somewhere new or meeting new people, my stomach knots up - like I'm doing something wrong by trying to move forward.
therapist: "That physical heaviness sounds overwhelming—like your body is holding onto the grief even when your mind tries to move forward. When those knots come up about meeting new people, what's the worst part your mind tells you about what that would mean?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: The worst part is thinking that if I start enjoying life again, it means I didn’t really love her. Like moving on would erase everything we had together. I know that’s probably not true, but it still feels that way deep down.
therapist: "You're describing such a painful paradox—that the love feels so real, the thought of joy almost threatens its memory. Your voice sounds like it's carrying both the weight of that fear and a quiet urgency to be understood. What would it feel like if someone could prove to you that moving forward doesn't erase what you shared?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess it would feel... relieving, but I don’t know how to believe that. Even if someone said it, it’s like my heart wouldn’t accept it. I think part of me wants to hold onto the pain because it feels like proof of how much she meant to me. Letting go scares me—what if I forget her?
therapist: "That fear of forgetting her—it sounds like the pain has become almost sacred, the last thread keeping her close. When you imagine relief, does part of you worry it would feel like losing her all over again, just in a different way?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, exactly. The pain feels like the only thing left that's ours. If I start feeling better, it's like she's slipping away for real this time. I know I should want to heal, but part of me is terrified of what happens when the hurt fades—who am I without this grief?
therapist: "It sounds like the grief has become intertwined with your sense of self—like letting it go would mean losing not just Maria, but a part of who you've become since the breakup. What might it look like to hold onto your memories of her while also making space for new parts of yourself to grow?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know—it feels like those two things can’t exist together. Either I’m stuck in the past holding onto her, or I move on and leave her behind. The idea of doing both sounds impossible, like trying to walk in two directions at once. How do I even start?
therapist: "That either/or feeling sounds exhausting—like you're being pulled between two impossible choices. Your voice speeds up when you describe this dilemma, as if the thought itself is overwhelming. What if there was a way to carry her with you *while* stepping forward—what might that look like, even just a tiny bit?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Maybe... I could start by going hiking again but bringing something that reminds me of her, like her favorite coffee thermos. But I don’t know—what if it just makes me feel worse? Sometimes trying to hold onto her while moving forward feels like reopening the wound every time.
therapist: "That sounds like a meaningful but scary first step—bringing something that honors her while reclaiming something you loved. When you imagine holding that thermos on the trail, what comes up? The concern about reopening the wound makes me wonder if you're expecting the pain to feel endless if you invite it in."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I can already picture myself sitting on our usual rock with that thermos and just... crumbling. But maybe that's not the worst thing? At least it would be real instead of this numb avoidance. Still, the idea terrifies me—what if I can't stop crying once I start? What if I ruin the trail for myself forever?
therapist: "You're describing such a vulnerable possibility—that allowing the grief in might feel overwhelming, but also more honest than numbness. Your voice tightens when you imagine crying there, like anticipating it might undo you completely. What if crumbling on that rock isn't ruining the trail, but reclaiming it—pain and all?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
